An asteroid is classified as potentially hazardous when its orbit comes within about 7.5 million km of Earth\'s orbit and it is large enough (roughly 140 m or bigger) to cause significant damage on impact. It\'s a broad safety classification based on orbit and size — not a prediction that this specific asteroid will hit Earth.

Sentry is a NASA/JPL system that continuously monitors near-Earth asteroid orbits for any not-yet-ruled-out chance of impact over roughly the next 100 years. Being tracked by Sentry means its orbit needs long-term monitoring — not that an impact is likely.
This isn\'t the asteroid\'s current distance from Earth. It\'s how close it will get on its closest approach date, shown in the Approach row above.
LD stands for Lunar Distance — roughly 384,400 km, the average distance between Earth and the Moon. It\'s used throughout this screen as an intuitive unit for how close an asteroid\'s approach is.
Shows only asteroids passing within 1 lunar distance (LD) — the threshold CNEOS uses to flag particularly close approaches.

Shows only asteroids at least 140 m across — the official size threshold NASA/CNEOS and ESA/NEOCC use for potentially hazardous asteroids. Since NASA reports size as a range, this checks the lower bound, so only asteroids that are large even under the most conservative estimate are shown.
